questions.stem: If \(P(x)=x\left(x^{2}-1\right)^{2}\), show that \(P(1)=P'(1)=0\). Which working is correct?
options: \(P(1)=1\left(1^{2}-1\right)^{2}=0\). So \(x=1\) is a root, and hence \(P'(1)=0\) as well.
questions.hint: Evaluate \(P(1)\) directly. For \(P'(x)\) use the product rule on \(x\cdot\left(x^{2}-1\right)^{2}\) with the chain rule for the square, then notice a common factor \(\left(x^{2}-1\right)\) which is 0 at \(x=1\).

steps.explain: Product rule: \(u=x\), \(u'=1\); \(v=\left(x^{2}-1\right)^{2}\), \(v'=2\left(x^{2}-1\right)\cdot2x\) (chain rule: derivative of the inside \(x^{2}-1\) is \(2x\)).
Take out the common factor \(\left(x^{2}-1\right)\): the first term leaves \(\left(x^{2}-1\right)\), the second leaves \(4x^{2}\).
Substitute \(x=1\): the first factor \(1^{2}-1=0\), so the whole product is 0.

Why not the others: B forgets the \(x\) factor in the product rule; C is not a proof (a root does not by itself give \(P'=0\) — it works here because the root is DOUBLE); D differentiates only the squared bracket.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Product rule plus chain rule; the factor x squared minus 1 is zero at x = 1.

steps.explain: \(x\)-intercepts: \(x=1\) (factor cubed: crosses with a flat point of inflexion), \(x=-2\) (factor squared: TOUCHES and turns), \(x=3\) (single: crosses).
\(y\)-intercept: put \(x=0\).
End behaviour: the leading term is \((-x)^{3}\cdot x^{2}\cdot(-x)=+x^{6}\), degree 6 with positive coefficient, so \(y\to+\infty\) at BOTH ends.

Signs between the roots: for \(x<-2\) and \(-2<x<1\) the curve is above the axis; for \(1<x<3\) it is below (\((1-x)^{3}<0\) and \((3-x)>0\)); for \(x>3\) it is above. So: down to touch \((-2,0)\), up through \((0,12)\), down through the flat point \((1,0)\), a minimum below the axis, then up through \((3,0)\).
Why not the others: B is a cubic (every root crosses once, \(y\)-intercept 6); C is upside down; D has the multiplicities swapped (it flattens at \(-2\) and touches at 1).
So the correct choice is option A.

questions.stem: \(P(x)=x^{3}-6x^{2}+ax-4\) where \(a>0\). Given that all the roots of \(P(x)\) are real and positive, and that one of the roots is the product of the other two roots, find the value of \(a\).
questions.hint: Call the roots \(\alpha,\beta,\alpha\beta\). Use the sum of roots, the sum of products in pairs, and the product of roots of a cubic \(x^{3}+bx^{2}+cx+d\): \(-b\), \(c\), \(-d\).

steps.explain: Let the roots be \(\alpha\), \(\beta\) and \(\gamma\), where \(\gamma=\alpha\beta\) (one root is the product of the other two). For \(x^{3}-6x^{2}+ax-4\): sum of roots \(=-(-6)=6\), sum of pairs \(=a\), product \(=-(-4)=4\).
From (3): \(\alpha\cdot\beta\cdot(\alpha\beta)=\alpha^{2}\beta^{2}=(\alpha\beta)^{2}=4\).
All roots are positive, so \(\alpha\beta>0\): reject \(-2\).
Substitute \(\alpha\beta=2\) into (1) to find \(\alpha+\beta\).
Now (2): factorise the last two terms: \(\alpha^{2}\beta+\alpha\beta^{2}=\alpha\beta(\alpha+\beta)\).
Substitute \(\alpha\beta=2\) and \(\alpha+\beta=4\).

Check the roots are real and positive: \(\alpha+\beta=4\) and \(\alpha\beta=2\) give \(\alpha,\beta=2\pm\sqrt{2}\) (both positive), and the third root is 2. Product: \((2+\sqrt{2})(2-\sqrt{2})(2)=2\times 2=4\) ✓.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Use sum, pairs and product of the roots with the roots alpha, beta and alpha beta.
